title: What changed
dek: Most family archives publish only what they found. This one publishes what it looked for, what it found, what it did not find, and what it had to take back.
lead: This page is the archive's working record. Each entry is one research pass: the sources opened, what came out of them, and which pages of this site changed as a result. Where a pass produced an error that was later corrected, it says so and links to the correction rather than quietly editing the history.

days.title: The maiden name, settled five times over
did: Searched the Queensland death index by MOTHER's name rather than by the deceased — the search this archive should have run a week ago.
Found five of Hannah's children's death registrations, each naming her, across 41 years and four spellings.
Found Hannah's own registration, naming her father John Saniger — entered by the clerk as “John Jenniger”.
Found James Wakefield's registration, naming HIS father Richard Wakefield: a new generation.
Found Miriam's marriage to William Hartley Sneyd, 15 November 1859, and corrected her age from twenty-one to nineteen.
Added 14 records and 9 recorded relationships to the register.
Asked Madeley for the two Sneyd baptisms the tree actually names — 1746 and 1769 — and found neither, in a parish transcribed continuously with 110 Sneyd records.
days.found: The archive spent a week trying to prove “Saniger” from the English end. It was written down five times in Queensland by five different clerks, and nobody had thought to search the index by the mother's name.

days.title: Portsea, Madeley, and three counties that hold nothing
did: Found Joseph D'Arcy baptised at Portsea St Mary on 19 March 1780, father Robert, mother Jean — the first record of Robert D'Arcy in an English parish register this archive has ever had.
Read the Madeley baptism that killed the Keele graft, and then found a William son of William Sneyd buried there in September 1744.

Established that FreeREG holds nothing for County Limerick, nothing for South Leith and nothing for St Quivox — three of this archive's oldest dead ends are dead ends in the database, not in the record.
Tested and rejected the Berkley-in-Somerset hypothesis for Hannah Saniger.
days.found: Robert D'Arcy and Jean Ward, named together as the parents of a child baptised at Portsea in 1780. His parentage is still unknown; his marriage is no longer a claim.

days.title: The Saniger chain, tested at last — and it breaks
did: Checked FreeREG's coverage for Bristol BEFORE searching it. Four registers, 1,551 records, and St Paul is not among them — so the Wakefield join was never testable there and any null would have been a lie.
Found that Dursley St James (1577–1951) and Cam St George (1568–1939) cover the whole Saniger chain, which /berkeley had implied was untestable.
Searched the county: 494 Saniger records 1670–1830, and three baptisms matching the tree's dates almost exactly, all at Dursley.
Opened all three. The fathers are Abraham, John and Samuel — three unrelated men. The chain is a coincidence of dates.
Established that no Saniger baptism exists in Gloucestershire 1801–1809, in a window that is well covered.
Established that in 139 Gloucestershire records spanning 1790–1900, no Saniger ever marries a Wakefield.
Found Miriam Wakefield's birth registration in FreeBMD: June quarter 1840, Bristol, volume 11, page 183 — the only one in England in five years.
Control-tested the FreeBMD harness (21,248 Wakefield marriages, 1838–1842) before reporting any absence from it.
Rewrote /berkeley around the result and added the GRO certificate to /errands as the cheapest decisive document on the site.

Then found the household in the 1841 census and published /drivers-fields — James and Hannah Wakefield at St Paul, Bristol, with Miriam aged one, and a seventy-year-old Sinegar widow living with them.
days.found: Three Dursley baptisms match the tree's dates for the middle of the Saniger line. Opening them shows three different fathers. The oldest claim in this archive is weaker than it was this morning — and for the first time there is a £2.50 document that would settle it. And then the census produced the couple themselves, at the street the tree had remembered and the county it had got wrong.

days.title: The DNA, and the branding brought into line
did: Published /dna — one living descendant's autosomal estimate against the tree's own prediction, computed twice, once with both grafts cut.
Corrected an error in that analysis within the hour: the first version put the predicted Scottish share at 0.02% and announced the DNA was contradicting the tree. It was not. Recorded as error nine.
Brought the homepage onto the .hero banner every sibling archive uses. The rules had been in this site's stylesheet, unused, since it was built.
Built /search over the whole archive, with the eleven spellings of Saniger folded together.
Added /searched, /changes and /errands — publishing work that had been sitting in notes/ and requests/ on disk.
days.found: That cutting both grafts — 98 people, thirteen generations, four royal houses — moves the predicted ancestry by 0.39 of a percentage point.

days.title: Berkeley, and the audit that moved the floor
did: Searched the Gloucestershire parish registers instead of another family's website.
Published /berkeley: 44 Sainger entries, three Williams, one good candidate and a father the archive never had.
Caught a false story before publishing it as fact, and left it on the page as a worked example.
Audited every 'defended' ancestor and published the result even though it was bad.
days.found: Of 144 ancestors the archive called documented, eight rest on a record set. Above generation seven, exactly one of sixty does. The honest figure is about seven generations, not twelve.

days.title: The worst error, and the register
did: Told the family their own founding brief was wrong. It was not; I had read the root person's spouse instead of her parents. It stood on the site for a day.
Published /register — every named individual the archive has met anywhere, with the source beside each one.
Put a pedigree chart on all 473 person pages, with the border encoding how each relationship is known.
days.found: Of 473 pedigree charts, 19 contain a single edge written in a record.

days.title: The inquest nobody knew about
did: Read QSA coronial file DR103140 in full and published it plainly at /inquest-1902.
Published /finding-arthur from the Red Cross file.
Rewrote /great-war around four men instead of one.
days.found: A suicide in Victoria Park in 1902 — and, in the widow's sworn deposition, the name of his father, closing a generation four research passes had been circling.

close: If you find something this page does not record, that is a gap in the record-keeping and worth telling me about.
